idiom_name: printf-family emitters: hand-written output functions over model structs
implementation_notes: C has no template facility in its standard library, so the classic structure is written by hand: the request handler (or CGI program) holds the model or query results and emits markup through printf/snprintf/fputs into the response stream. stdio knows only conversion specifiers such as %s and %d - it has no notion of HTML - so every value that reaches the output must pass through an escaping helper you also write, and a format string must never be data, because fprintf(out, user_input) is a format-string vulnerability rather than a template. The hand-written form remains justified for CGI-style tools, embedded device pages and code paths where a template engine dependency is unacceptable; once pages multiply, generate them outside C or embed a small engine such as mustache.
pitfalls: printf writes exactly what it is given: %s inserts a name verbatim, so html_escape() is required at every call site and forgetting one is the injection hole.
sprintf into a fixed buffer overflows when the page grows; use snprintf (C99), check its return value and handle truncation, or stream with fprintf/fputs.
A non-literal format string (fprintf(out, user_supplied)) is a format-string vulnerability - pass user data as an argument, never as the format.
C strings are NUL-terminated views into memory you own: emitting a field after free() or a realloc invalidation is silent corruption, and no engine will copy the value for you.
